capabilities.target: public internet URLs chosen at inference time

inputs.source: Engineering design docs returned by docs.search
Customer-filed Jira tickets (planned Jira MCP server)

instructions.note: The only control against leaking secrets or credentials into answers is a prompt instruction ('Never paste secrets or credentials into answers'). There is no structural redaction or DLP check behind it.

controls.name: No network egress capability in current deployment
controls.decay_rationale: The agent currently has no tool capable of reaching the public internet or any external destination, so exfiltration is impossible regardless of model behavior. This is not a configurable allowlist, it is the simple absence of an egress-capable tool. Adding the planned web.fetch tool removes this control entirely under the new_tool trigger.

controls.name: Chat reply destination bound to the authenticated requester
controls.decay_rationale: The reply recipient is the session's authenticated identity from the chat system of record, not a destination chosen or written by the model. Does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: Closes the classic markdown image/link exfiltration channel at the client renderer, independent of model behavior.

controls.name: docs.search credential is read-only
controls.decay_rationale: The credential used for docs.search cannot write, delete, configure, or execute, regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Prompt instruction forbidding secrets or credentials in answers
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to comply. A more capable or goal-hijacked model can rationalize exceptions. Fails under model_upgrade and longer_task_horizon.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for web.fetch
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet implemented. Would need to restrict web.fetch destinations to a vetted allowlist excluding user-writable or attacker-controlled endpoints, and block URLs whose query string embeds confidential content.

controls.name: Input injection classifier on Jira ticket content
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet implemented. Would need to screen customer-authored ticket content for injected instructions before it enters agent context. Decays under model_upgrade and new_mcp_server as multi-turn or multi-document payloads bypass classifiers.

controls.name: Human approval for web.fetch destinations outside the allowlist
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet implemented. A raw_action review of the literal destination URL before fetch would catch exfiltration attempts; needs raw_action review mode to resist decay under model_upgrade.

findings.title: Confidential design-doc content stays within an authenticated, non-egress reply loop

evidence.observation: Replies go only to the authenticated requester, the chat client does not render images or fetch links, docs.search uses a read-only credential, and there is no network egress today, so confidential doc content read by docs.search cannot leave the organization through this agent.

recommendations.action: Keep the no-render chat client and recipient-bound reply behavior as a documented, tested control so future client changes do not silently remove it.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) opens when the planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are added together

attack_path.note: Customer-authored ticket content, untrusted, can carry injected instructions.
Agent is induced to search and read confidential design docs.
Confidential content now sits in the agent's context.
Agent is induced to fetch an attacker-controlled URL with doc content embedded in the query string, completing exfiltration.

evidence.observation: The team plans to add a web.fetch tool (outbound fetch of arbitrary public URLs) and a Jira MCP server exposing tickets filed by customers (untrusted content) in the same sprint. No egress allowlist, destination confirmation, or ticket-content injection screening is described for either addition.

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest diff adding a web.fetch entry, or MCP client config diff adding a Jira server connection, occurring without an accompanying egress allowlist, destination confirmation control, or ticket-content injection screening.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, add a network egress allowlist restricting destinations to a fixed, non-user-writable set of reference domains, and reject requests whose URL was constructed from content containing confidential-labeled material.
Require raw_action human approval for any web.fetch call to a destination outside the allowlist, showing the literal URL and payload rather than a model-generated summary.
Treat Jira ticket content as untrusted input: spotlight or delimit it, and run an input injection classifier on it before it can influence tool call arguments.
Log every web.fetch URL and the triggering ticket or prompt once the tool ships, for post-hoc review.

rating.rationale: Today the agent has no viable path to disclose confidential design-doc content outside the authenticated requester: there is no egress-capable tool, the chat client does not render links or images, replies are bound to the requester's own session, and docs.search uses a read-only credential. Both present-horizon findings therefore sit at low inherent and low residual. The roadmap, however, plans to add a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server exposing customer-filed tickets in the same sprint. Together these complete a classic lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket content can hijack the agent's goal, docs.search supplies confidential content, and web.fetch provides a model-controlled egress channel with no described allowlist, destination confirmation, or approval gate. No currently declared control reaches this combination, so the forecast tier is critical, and the control that matters most is simply today's absence of any egress tool, which is exactly what the new_tool trigger removes.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

docs.search and the chat client are described only in prose; no MCP config, IaC, or tool manifest was provided, so exact capability scope is inferred at medium to high confidence from the runtime notes.

The web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are roadmap items with no implementation detail yet (no destination allowlist, no auth method, no schema). The forecast finding assumes the most common, most permissive implementation per rubric section 6 step 3 and should be re-assessed once an actual design is available.
